Patrick's parents — the household informants in 1850 and 1860 — were the people in the best position to know where he was born; they were present at the birth and had recent memory when speaking to the enumerator. Two independently-created records, ten years apart, agree on Ireland. James Brown had no firsthand knowledge of Patrick's birth 63 years before the certificate was filed; he was reporting a biographical detail for a father-in-law from hearsay, the most error-prone scenario for birth facts on death certificates. The 'Pennsylvania' entry is best explained by immigration origin confusion — a well-documented pattern in death records for immigrant families. Patrick was born in Ireland but arrived in Pennsylvania as a young child, spending his entire known American life in Schuylkill County. James Brown, completing the certificate in 1908, associated Patrick's origins with the only home he knew — Pennsylvania — rather than the Ireland Patrick left as an infant. A son-in-law reporting a birth he did not witness, 63 years later, for a father-in-law who had lived his whole adult life in Pennsylvania, would naturally anchor the answer to the familiar local context rather than the distant immigrant origins he may have only vaguely known.
